translations.text: There was a certain rich man: and so on.
The Ruling Lord told this parable to his disciples, saying thus, "A certain wealthy man was adorned with purple and fine linen, and lived splendidly every day.
Then a certain poor man lay at his gate, and his name was Lazarus; he was a leper:" and so on.
This gospel has now been told simply. The holy pope Gregory revealed to us the hidden meaning of this reading.
He said, "The holy gospel did not say that the rich man was a robber, but that he was stingy and grew proud in his wealth."
From this we should consider how the man who robs another will be punished, when the man who would not give away his own for the love of God is condemned to hell.
This man's stinginess and pride sank him into living torment, because he had no mercy, by which he might have redeemed his own soul with his treasure.

Now some people think that there is no danger in costly garments; but if it were not a sin, the holy gospel would not have stated so clearly about the rich man that he was adorned with purple and with fine linen.
No one seeks out costlier clothing except for vain boasting, truly so that he may be ranked above other people because of his finery.
In another place the Lord praised John the Baptist for the harshness of his clothing, because he was clothed in camel's hair, poorly and roughly.
When the Saviour spoke about the rich man, he said, "There was a certain rich man." Then about the poor man: "There was a certain needy man called Lazarus."
You know that a rich man is better known among his people than a poor man; yet the Saviour did not name the wealthy man, but the beggar;
because the names of humble people are known to him through their election, but he does not know the proud, because they are rejected.

The rich man might have had some excuse for his stinginess if the leprous poor man had not lain before his eyes. It would also have been easier on the poor man's mind if he had not seen the rich man's wealth.
He endured many kinds of suffering, since he had neither food, nor health, nor clothing, and he saw the rich man, healthy and splendidly dressed, enjoying his delicacies.
His sickness would have been enough for the poor man even if he had had food; and his poverty would have been enough for him even if he had been healthy.
But his many hardships were the cleansing of his soul, and the rich man's stinginess and pride were his downfall, because he saw the other man's misery and despised him with a swollen, arrogant mind.
But when he was despised by men, the dogs came near and licked his wounds. A dog's licking heals wounds.
Then it happened that the poor man died, and angels carried his soul to the dwelling of the patriarch Abraham;
and after his death the rich man's spirit was sunk into hell. Then he wanted to have as his protector the man to whom he would not give his crumbs before.

Then with a wretched voice he begged Abraham that Lazarus might drip [water] on his tongue; but that little favour was not granted him, because earlier in life Lazarus had not been allowed to have the crumbs from his table.
He complained most about his tongue, because the wealthy commonly indulge in harmful jesting at their feasts;
So his tongue, as the just reward, was punished more bitterly for his idle talk.
The patriarch Abraham said to him, "You, my son, remember that in your life you received wealth, and Lazarus misery." This saying is more to be feared than to be explained.
If the rich man did any good, he was repaid with transitory riches; and if the poor man did any evil, he was repaid with misery.
So the wealthy man received his happiness as his reward, to enjoy for a short time, and the poor man's destitution cleansed away his little sins.
Poverty afflicted the one and cleansed him; abundance enriched the other and deceived him.
I beg you, dearest people, do not despise God's poor, even if they do something blameworthy;
for their misery cleanses what even a small excess defiles. Look carefully at each case, for it often happens that things go well for the wicked in this life.
The patriarch said to the wealthy man, "Between us and you a great gulf [?] is fixed; even if someone wishes [to go] from us to you, he cannot;

nor [can anyone come] from you to us either." The reprobate long with great eagerness to be allowed [out] of the torment in which they suffer, but the strength of hell's enclosure does not allow them ever to break out.
The saints too are so filled with their Creator's righteousness that they do not grieve at all over the misery of the reprobate;
because they see the damned as far estranged from themselves as they are thrust away from their beloved Lord.
After the rich man had lost hope of his own release, the memory of his brothers came into his mind;
for the punishment of the reprobate very often draws their minds uselessly to love, so that they then love their kinsmen, though earlier in life they loved neither themselves nor their kin.
He who binds himself with sins does not love himself. He recognized Lazarus, whom he had earlier despised, and he remembered his brothers, whom he had left behind;

For the poor man would not have been fully avenged on the rich man if the rich man had not recognized him while in his torment; and again, his torment in the fire would not have been complete unless he expected the same torments for his kinsmen.
The sinful sometimes see now the elect in glory, whom they despised in the world, so that the anguish of their minds may be the greater:

and the righteous always see the unrighteous suffering in their torments, so that their own bliss may be the greater, and their love for their Lord, who rescued them from the devil's power and from the wicked crowd.
What the righteous see stirs no fear in them, nor does it lessen their glory; for there will be no grieving there over the misery of the wicked.

but their torments become greater bliss for the chosen, just as in a painting the black figure is provided [? 'forsewen', literally 'looked over' or 'disregarded'] so that the white may be seen more brightly.
The elect always see the brightness of their Creator, and therefore nothing in creation is hidden from them.

The rich man would not listen in his lifetime to the teacher Moses or to God's prophets. So he also supposed that his brothers would despise them as he had done, and therefore he asked that Lazarus might warn them, so that they would not come to his torment.
The patriarch answered him, "If they despise the law of Moses and the preaching of the prophets, they will not believe, even if someone rises from death."
Those who neglect the easy commands of the old law, how then will they obey the lofty commands of the teaching of Christ, who rose from death?
I beg you, my brothers, to keep in mind Lazarus's rest and the rich man's punishment, and do as Christ himself taught: "Make friends for yourselves among God's poor,
"that they may receive you, at your ends, into eternal dwelling-places." You now have many Lazaruses lying at your gates, asking for what you have to spare.
Though they may seem contemptible, they will afterwards be your intercessors with the Almighty.
Truly we ought to entreat the poor to ask of us, for those who now beg and seek food from us are our protectors.
We must not despise their lowliness, for Christ is served when the poor are received, as he himself said, "I was hungry, and you fed me;
I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was naked, and you clothed me."
Now Saint Gregory says that there was a venerable monk in the land of Lycaonia, very devout; his name was Martyrius.

At his abbot's command he went on an errand to another monastery. On the way he found a leper lying there, all covered in cracked sores, who had no control of his feet. The leper said that he wanted to reach his hut, if he could.
Then the monk took pity on the leper's weakness, wrapped him in his cloak, and carried him toward the monastery.

Then it was revealed to his abbot whom he was carrying, and he cried out with a loud voice and said, "Run, run, and open the monastery gate quickly, for our brother Martyrius is carrying the Saviour on his back."
When the monk drew near to the monastery gate, the one who had seemed to be a leper slipped from his neck and was seen in the likeness of Christ.
Then the monk looked up and saw how he ascended to heaven. As he ascended, the Saviour said, "Martyrius, you were not ashamed of me on earth, and I am not ashamed of you in heaven."
Then the abbot hurried toward the monk and said earnestly, "My brother, where is the one you were carrying?"
He said, "If I had known who he was, I would have lain at his feet. When I carried him, I felt no weight of any burden."
How could he feel the weight of any burden, when he was carrying the one who bore him?
Now Saint Gregory says that the Saviour then confirmed the saying that he himself spoke: "What you do for the poor in my name, you do for me myself."
What in human nature is as glorious as Christ's humanity? And what in human nature seems more horrible than a leper's body, with its swelling, its sores, and its reeking stench?
But he who is worthy of honour above all creatures humbled himself to be seen in that hideous form, so that we should grieve over the misery of human beings,
and comfort them as far as we are able, for love of the merciful and humble Saviour, so that he may grant us a dwelling in his kingdom in eternal life, he who rescued us from the devil's captivity;
who reigns in eternity with the Almighty Father and the Holy Spirit, the three of them dwelling in one Godhead, without beginning and end, for ever and ever. Amen.
